transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-14
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Maya Li (Aurora Head of Platform), Ethan Ross (Aurora Backend), Carl Meyer (Aurora SRE), Jenna Park (Aurora PM)

Summary (auto):
Short demo focused on edge-case behavior: long context handling (50k+ tokens), very high TPS (target 1k-2k sustained), streaming backpressure and client timeouts. Showed Redwood Console trace and Optimize recommendations; discussed private vs dedicated routing, fallback model variants, and KMS/encryption concerns. Action items and follow-up POC scoping agreed.

Topics:
- Long context retention & KV/cache strategies
- High TPS load patterns, batching, autoscale policies
- Streaming backpressure and client-side timeouts
- Console observability (per-token latency, traces)
- Optimize suggestions (quantization, prefix caching)
- Security: VPC peering, KMS, audit logs

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: okay so thanks everyone for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, I'll kick it off. Uh, we scheduled 60 minutes to run through a targeted stress demo — long context, streaming behavior under load, and then walk the Console and Optimize recommendations. Priya and Liam are here to run the live parts.

[00:22] Maya Li: thanks Jordan. quick ask before we start: we want to reproduce our prod pattern — sessions that keep a 40k token history and then burst to 1k rps for a few minutes. can you show how Redwood handles that?

[00:35] Priya Desai: absolutely. we'll start by outlining the key limits and then kick off two parallel tests: a long-context inference stream and a high-TPS burst test. Heads-up, the demo will use a slightly smaller model variant for noise control but we'll show the same settings for your larger models.

[00:52] Ethan Ross: curious about memory — when you say "KV cache" how does that map to GPU memory and do you spill to host if it gets large?

[01:05] Priya Desai: good question. Redwood's runtime keeps the KV cache on GPU while possible; if sequence lengths/slots exceed capacity the runtime will either compact the cache or route to a compatible larger instance class. We do have a soft spill-to-host path but it's not ideal for latency — it's a throughput/latency tradeoff. (note: some words transcribed wrong, we said spill-to-host but sometimes internal team calls it host-swap or h-swap)

[01:35] Liam O'Connor: also worth noting that Optimize will recommend prefix caching for repeated system prompts which reduces per-request KV delta and helps you keep the live cache smaller over time.

[01:50] Carl Meyer: regarding routing — will requests get automatically re-routed to dedicated pools if a node is overloaded? we need resilient fallbacks without 503s.

[02:05] Priya Desai: yes, we have smart routing policies. in hosted mode we can failover to a cheaper/compatible model variant or route to dedicated capacity if you've reserved it. we can also set strict latency SLOs so requests drop to a lower-cost model before erroring out.

[02:33] Jenna Park: and how do you measure the client timeout interplay with streaming? our clients set a 10s websocket read deadline.

[02:45] Priya Desai: great— we'll demo streaming under backpressure. we'll show two behaviors: 1) server-side pacing — where Redwood batches tokens to maximize throughput while keeping steady pacing, and 2) backpressure handling — if the client can't keep up, we buffer up to a configured window and then apply a flow-control policy that can pause the generator or drop to smaller token chunks.

[03:10] Jordan Kim: ok let's move to demo part 1 — long context stream. Priya, can you start the console and load the test prompts?

[03:18] [00:03:18] Priya Desai: launching the Console recording now. I'll paste a link to the session artifacts in chat — small deck + load script. link: https://redwood.example.com/session/ff-20251014-demo-artifacts (demo link, not public)

[03:38] [00:03:38] Priya Desai: starting a single session with an approx 45k token system+chat history. hitting /v1/chat/completions stream mode, we set max_new_tokens 512 and enable prefix_cache=true + kv_compaction=on.

[04:05] [00:04:05] Maya Li: just to flag, our real sessions sometimes append very large documents mid-session — we want to see how the runtime reacts when the context jumps.

[04:18] [00:04:18] Priya Desai: copying a 100k token doc into the session now to force compaction. you might see a small spike in tokens-per-second as compaction runs.

[04:37] [00:04:37] Developer Voice (transcript): oh — okay that's interesting, uh the console shows the sequence length jumped and the kernel selector recompiled to the wider attention kernel. That caused a ~120ms latency bump per token for the next 2k tokens.

[05:05] [00:05:05] Ethan Ross: 120ms per token sounds... that's a lot if you have many tokens. how does that amortize across the session?

[05:20] Priya Desai: it only spikes when we change kernel or reallocate big KV pages. after compaction the per-token latency returns to normal. Optimize will flag these events in traces and recommend either warm-up patterns or pre-provisioning for expected context jumps.

[05:45] [00:05:45] Liam O'Connor: showing the trace view — you can see the kernel switch at 00:04:37 and the correlating increase in GPU memcpy times. Also calling out the per-token cost delta in the Console's cost breakdown.

[06:10] [00:06:10] Maya Li: is there an option to pause token generation during compaction to avoid delivering degraded token latencies to the client?

[06:22] Priya Desai: yes we support a policy that pauses the generation and returns a short system message to the client to signal maintenance-window style behavior — many customers prefer that to gradual latency spikes. That's configurable per-route.

[06:40] Jordan Kim: quick Q from legal/security: do you log raw history or only token hashes in the audit trail?

[06:52] Liam O'Connor: by default we log metadata and token-counts; raw payload logging is disabled unless you opt-in for debugging. For Private deployments we can integrate with customer KMS and make sure logs are encrypted at rest and in transit.

[07:08] [00:07:08] Demo stage 2: high TPS load.

[07:15] Priya Desai: kicking off the throughput test now. We'll try a sustained 1k rps for 2 minutes, then a 2k rps 30s burst. We'll run with batching enabled and with the adaptive batch size policy that Optimize suggests.

[07:42] [00:07:42] Priya Desai: starting load generator... note the generator uses synthetic prompts that approximate your average payload size of ~400 tokens request + response.

[08:02] [00:08:02] Console Voice: incoming rps 1000, average latency 210ms per request, batching factor 12, token throughput 85k tokens/s (est).

[08:20] Ethan Ross: wow 85k tokens/s — is that across a pool or per-instance?

[08:28] Liam O'Connor: that's aggregate across a small dedicated pool we spun for the demo. Per-instance numbers vary on GPU type; Optimize will recommend instance size and quantization profile for your realistic workload.

[08:50] [00:08:50] Priya Desai: 30s into the sustained 1k rps — looking at per-route trace, there's steady batching and tokenization overheads flatten out. No 5xxs so far.

[09:15] [00:09:15] Carl Meyer: what happens when a single client opens many concurrent streams? do you have head-of-line blocking?

[09:28] Priya Desai: we use per-connection flow control and per-tenant queuing. If one connection is slow it won't block unrelated connections — the runtime groups requests by routing key and shuffles batches to avoid head-of-line scenarios. There can still be contention on KV cache if many sessions reference very large shared histories.

[09:58] [00:09:58] Priya Desai: ok switching to burst to 2k rps now. you might see more aggressive batching and some adaptive autoscale action.

[10:18] [00:10:18] Console Voice: burst to 2000 rps detected, spin-up recommended to avoid SLO misses; autoscaler pre-warming 3 nodes from warm pool.

[10:30] [00:10:30] Ethan Ross: can pre-warming cause double billing if nodes sit idle afterward?

[10:40] Jordan Kim: good practical note — our reserved capacity and burst policies allow you to cap pre-warm limits. You can also set fallback to cheaper model variants to avoid over-provisioning. We'll send pricing examples in the follow-up.

[10:58] [00:10:58] Demo: streaming backpressure scenario.

[11:05] Priya Desai: now we'll simulate a slow websocket client: small read window and intermittent network — this will exercise backpressure buffering.

[11:25] [00:11:25] Console Voice: buffering 450 KB for connection id a3f... applying flow-control pause after buffer threshold (1500 KB) reached.

[11:40] Developer Voice: the buffer threshold hit at ~00:11:25; runtime applied chunked streaming (200 token chunks) and added a keepalive event to the client. You can also set a policy to drop and return a 429 or to throttle generation.

[12:02] Jenna Park: if client timeouts are 10s, and you're chunking, how many chunks before the client times out? are the chunks guaranteed within that window?

[12:20] Priya Desai: chunk delivery depends on model latency; we can configure target chunk latency via console route settings. If a client times out you can opt to resume the session later — we persist KV state so a resumed session can continue without a full recompute. There's a tradeoff: persisting KV state increases storage/retention cost.

[12:46] Maya Li: might be a dealbreaker for us if resume adds >200ms overhead. what's typical resume cost?

[12:58] Liam O'Connor: resume cost for warm cached states is usually under 50ms; for cold state with disk spill it's higher and depends on host swap. Optimize will model these numbers given your session distribution.

[13:22] [00:13:22] Priya Desai: quick aside — some internal transcripts use the term "KV cache shrink" which the console shows as "KV compaction". apologies for inconsistency in the UI text in this demo environment.

[13:45] [00:13:45] Carl Meyer: curious about tracing retention — how long do you keep sample traces that show kernel switches? we need 90 days for audits.

[13:58] Liam O'Connor: observability retention is configurable; for hosted customers we offer 30/90/365 day tiers. For Private we can mirror your retention SLAs. All traces can be exported to your SIEM.

[14:20] [00:14:20] Priya Desai: now jumping into the Console UI — I'll show the per-route dashboard, token heatmap, and the Optimize tab which suggests quantization levels and adaptive batching settings.

[14:42] [00:14:42] Priya Desai: for this workload Optimize recommends 4-bit quantization for the model family you're considering and an adaptive batch size target of 10-16 for the 400-token average. It also suggests enabling prefix caching for 70% of sessions.

[15:05] Ethan Ross: 4-bit — do you see quality regressions with our long-context prompts? we rely on faithful retrieval of chunks from the 100k doc.

[15:20] Liam O'Connor: there can be minor degens on specific tasks; Optimize includes a regression check tied to your eval set. We recommend A/Bing a quantized variant in canary for a week.

[15:42] Jordan Kim: demo note — we'll attach the Optimize report after the call with the expected latency/cost delta across profiles.

[16:05] [00:16:05] Priya Desai: next demo bit: timeouts under heavy GC / kernel recompile events. We'll artificially trigger kernel selector change by toggling sequence length and observe the effect on streaming windows.

[16:28] [00:16:28] Console Voice: kernel recompile event at 00:16:20, observed 95ms increase in 99th percentile token latency for 4s.

[16:45] Maya Li: if a kernel recompile hits mid-stream and the client times out, will Redwood re-stream the missing tokens upon client reconnect?

[16:58] Priya Desai: we persist generator state so yes — reconnects can pick up where they left off if you keep the session identifier. We also support idempotency keys to deduplicate replays.

[17:22] [00:17:22] Demo pause for Q/A

[17:30] Carl Meyer: on the private deployment path, do you support air-gapped clusters where Redwood control-plane calls home are blocked?

[17:42] Liam O'Connor: we have an offline installer and control plane proxy options. Some customers run a completely isolated inference plane with a local control plane and an optional one-way reporting channel for billing/telemetry. We can share the private deploy notes.

[18:05] Jenna Park: about security docs — can you provide SOC2 artifacts and encryption diagrams?

[18:15] Jordan Kim: yes, action item — we'll send SOC2 and the private deployment security pack. see action items.

[18:30] [00:18:30] Priya Desai: switching to a synthetic failure scenario: sudden node failure during 1k rps sustained. we'll kill a node and watch routing/fallback.

[18:48] Console Voice: node n-7 removed, routing redistributed, observed 1.8% increase in tail latency for 30s, no 5xxs as requests routed to warm pool.

[19:10] Ethan Ross: so you guarantee no 5xxs? that's a strong SLA language — what's the fallback window?

[19:22] Jordan Kim: we guarantee availability per SLA for Dedicated customers; for hosted we have SLOs and will provide failure-mode docs. specifics will be part of the contract for Reserved pools.

[19:50] [00:19:50] Priya Desai: running a quick show of Console logs — you can filter by request id, see kernel switches, KV pressure events, and a per-token cpu/gpu breakdown.

[20:15] Maya Li: ok this is helpful. real ask: can you produce a runbook for our on-call that explains the thresholds and remediation steps for the common edge-cases you showed?

[20:30] Priya Desai: yes — we'll include a runbook draft and tie it to the Optimize recommendations; action item captured.

[20:52] [00:20:52] Demo wrap-up — performance summary.

[21:00] Liam O'Connor: summary numbers from the session: sustained 1k rps with avg latency 210ms, burst 2k rps handled with autoscale pre-warm, long-context compaction spikes ~120ms per token during kernel recompile events, buffer/backpressure handled with chunking and flow-control policies, resume typically under 50ms for warm state.

[21:32] Maya Li: those numbers look promising. our procurement and infra teams will want documented evidence; can you provide the raw CSVs and the Console recording?

[21:45] Jordan Kim: yes, next steps include sharing the CSVs, recording, and a tailored Optimize report. we'll also scope a POC to run your real prompts with full model variants on your schedule.

[22:05] Ethan Ross: last technical q — in private mode, how do upgrades work? do you have rolling kernel upgrades that can cause short regen pauses?

[22:18] Liam O'Connor: upgrades are rolling and we provide upgrade windows; small windows where kernel recompile occurs can affect token latency briefly, but we can schedule them during maintenance windows and pre-warm post-upgrade.

[22:40] Jenna Park: what about cost? can Optimize show the cost delta if we choose to keep longer session retention vs shorter?

[22:52] Priya Desai: yes — Optimize will show cost per 1M tokens and modeled cost for your session retention policies. We'll include that in the follow-up.

[23:15] [00:23:15] Quick note: a few lines in the Console rendered the product name as "Reedwood" in this test environment — ignore the typo in the UI demo.

[23:30] Jordan Kim: ok let's recap next steps and owners.

[23:35] Jordan Kim: recap: Jordan will send SOC2 + pricing + console recording; Priya will run the 2k TPS sim with Aurora's sample prompts and share CSVs; Ethan will send representative long-context corpus; we'll schedule POC scoping week of 2025-10-27. Anything to add?

[23:58] Maya Li: that's it from Aurora. thanks for the thorough walkthrough.

[24:05] Jordan Kim: great — thanks everyone. we'll follow up by end of day with the artifacts.
